183.title: Pauri 12, meaning: beyond describing
183.hook: the state of the one who trusts cannot be described; there is no paper or pen for it (Japji 12)
183.howItsDone: Pauri 12 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning by many Sikhs; its closing lines on the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts, return as the refrain of pauris 12 to 15.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new word: mannai. Your line was mannai, trusting. Did you take one piece of advice to heart and follow it? Today, what that first line of Pauri 12 actually says. Day one hundred eighty-three.

Try to explain to someone why you trust your oldest friend. You start listing things. She showed up when my car broke down. He kept a secret for ten years. And halfway through the list, you can hear it's not landing. The facts are true, but they're not the thing. The thing is the ease in your shoulders when that person walks in, and there's no sentence for that. Anyone who has tried to describe being in love, or holding a newborn, knows the feeling of words running out. Pauri 12 says the same happens to the one who trusts, and then it says something bold about writing.
screen: `WHY DO YOU TRUST HER?` → `THE LIST DOESN'T LAND.` → `WORDS RUN OUT.`

segments.voice: Here is Pauri 12, in paraphrase. The state of the one who trusts cannot be told. Whoever tries to tell it regrets it afterward. There's no paper, no pen, no writer who can sit down and capture the state of the one who trusts. Such is the Name of the Stainless One. Only someone who trusts knows it, in their own mind. Four moves. First, the state can't be told. We heard that line yesterday: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Second, the one who tries regrets it. Not because trying is wrong, but because every description comes out smaller than the thing, and you feel the shrinking as you speak. Third, and this is the surprising one, there's no paper and no pen for it: kaagad kalam na likhanhaar. Paper, pen, writer, all three named and all three set aside. Remember where this is written. Japji stands at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib, a book Sikhs treat with enormous reverence, carried on the head, wrapped in cloth, read aloud with care. And inside that book, Guru Nanak says writing can't hold this. The scripture points past itself. Fourth, the refrain that will close each of these four trusting stanzas: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. That's not a secret handshake. It's more like swimming. You can read about water all day. You only know it from inside.
screen: `THE STATE CANNOT BE TOLD.` · `WHOEVER TRIES, REGRETS.` · `NO PAPER, NO PEN, NO WRITER.` · `KNOWN ONLY FROM INSIDE.` · then, large: `NO PEN FOR THIS.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, trust one thing without explaining it. Maybe the chair holding you. Maybe the next breath arriving on its own. Let your weight go into the seat. Let the breath come without managing it. Each time your mind starts to explain why it's safe to trust, drop the explanation and just rest. You don't need the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 12. The state of the one who trusts can't be told; no paper, no pen, no writer can hold it. It's known from inside.
Your line: no pen for this. Today, when something moves you and the words won't come, don't force them. Let it stay bigger than the sentence. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: Pauri 13: trusting, awareness
184.hook: mannai: by trust the mind becomes aware and knows all realms (Japji 13)
184.tomorrow: Pauri 14: trusting, the path is clear
184.howItsDone: Pauri 13 is part of the morning Japji; many Sikhs speak of surat, awareness, being joined to the shabad as the center of their practice, especially while listening to kirtan or reciting the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 12: the one who trusts can't be described. Your line was no pen for this. Did something stay bigger than your words? Today, what trusting does to the mind. Day one hundred eighty-four.

You'd think trust would make you sleepy. Relax, you've got this, lean back. But watch a child on a parent's shoulders at a parade. Because she's safe up there, she sees everything: the drummers, the balloons, the dog in the crowd. The child on the ground, gripping a hand and worried about getting lost, sees knees. Safety doesn't dull her. It frees her attention to look around. Pauri 13 makes a claim like that. Trusting doesn't put the mind to sleep. It wakes it up.
screen: `A CHILD ON A PARENT'S SHOULDERS.` → `SAFE, SO SHE SEES EVERYTHING.` → `TRUST WAKES THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Pauri 13 opens: mannai surat hovai man budh. By trusting, surat comes into the mind and the understanding. Surat is today's word, and it's one of the great words of Sikh teaching. It means awareness, attention, consciousness, the part of you that is awake and noticing. In Sikh thought, surat is what attunes to the shabad, the Word, the way a radio tunes to a station. The Gurus speak of surat joined to shabad as the heart of the path. Then the pauri goes on, in paraphrase. By trusting, one knows of all the realms, every world. By trusting, one doesn't take blows to the face. By trusting, one doesn't go off with the messenger of death. And the refrain: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. Notice the order. Awareness comes first. Before knowing all realms, before escaping fear, the first gift of trust is that you wake up. That fits what we've heard. Listening gave direction; trusting gives attention. And it fits an ordinary Tuesday. When you're anxious, your attention shrinks to one tight spot, the worry. When you trust, it opens. You notice the light on the wall, the tone in someone's voice, what the moment is actually asking. The blows to the face and the messenger of death are the stanza's picture of fear itself. A mind that trusts doesn't flinch at every shadow. It has room to see.
screen: `MANNAI SURAT HOVAI MAN BUDH.` · `SURAT — AWARENESS, ATTENTION.` · `AWARENESS COMES FIRST.` · `FEAR SHRINKS, TRUST OPENS.` · then, large: `TRUST WAKES YOU.`

segments.voice: Be aware of your whole body, once. Start at the top of your head and let attention move down slowly: face, jaw, shoulders, arms, hands, chest, belly, hips, legs, feet. Don't fix anything. Just notice. When you reach your feet, try to feel the whole body at once, one shape, breathing. Rest there. If the mind narrows onto a worry, widen it again to the whole body. The bell holds the time.
Surat. Awareness, attention, the waking consciousness that tunes to the Word. By trusting, Pauri 13 says, surat comes.
Your line: trust wakes you. Today, when you feel safe for a moment, don't just relax: look around, and notice three things you'd normally miss. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: Pauri 14: trusting, the path is clear
185.hook: mannai: by trust the path is not blocked and one walks with honor (Japji 14)
185.tomorrow: Pauri 15: trusting, the door of freedom
185.howItsDone: Pauri 14 is recited as part of Japji Sahib in the Sikh morning Nitnem; many Sikhs hear its four mannai lines as a description of living openly and rightly out of trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surat, awareness. Your line was trust wakes you. Did you notice three things you'd usually miss? Today, trust starts to walk. Day one hundred eighty-five.

There's an email you haven't answered. Or a call you keep meaning to make, a doctor's appointment you keep not booking, an apology sitting in your drafts. It's been there so long it feels like a wall. Every day you walk up to it, look at it, and turn around. And then one day you just do it, and the strange thing is how small it was. The wall was mostly fear. Once you step, the road behind it is ordinary road. Pauri 14 is about that road. It says that for the one who trusts, the path isn't blocked.
screen: `THE EMAIL YOU HAVEN'T ANSWERED.` → `IT FEELS LIKE A WALL.` → `ONE STEP, AND IT'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Pauri 14 has four short lines, each beginning with mannai, by trusting. The first, in the original: mannai maarag thaak na paae. Maarag is the road, the way. Thaak is a block, a barrier, something that stops you. By trusting, the road meets no barrier. The second, in paraphrase: by trusting, one goes forth with honor, openly, in full view. Pat is honor, and the picture is of someone who doesn't have to sneak. The third: by trusting, one doesn't wander off down side roads. Commentators read this as not being pulled here and there by every passing path, ritual or fashion. The fourth: by trusting, one is bound to dharma, to right living. Then the refrain again: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. So the stanza draws a road. It's clear, you walk it openly, you don't drift off it, and it's tied to doing right. What's worth noticing is what the pauri doesn't promise. It doesn't say the road will be easy, or short, or free of hills. It says it won't be blocked. The pauri doesn't list the barriers. Many readers hear in them the ones fear builds: hesitation, doubt, the sense that you'll be seen and judged. On that reading, trust takes those down. And one more thing. The first gift of trust, yesterday, was awareness. Today's is movement. Wake up, then walk. Japji keeps building step on step.
screen: `MAARAG — THE ROAD. THAAK — A BLOCK.` · `GOING FORTH WITH HONOR.` · `NO WANDERING DOWN SIDE ROADS.` · `BOUND TO DHARMA.` · then, large: `THE WAY OPENS.`

segments.voice: Think of one step you've been avoiding. Not the whole project, just the first step: the first line of the email, the number you need to dial. Picture yourself taking it, simply, in full view. Notice where fear sits in your body when you picture it, and breathe into that spot. Then decide when today you'll take the step. For the rest of the time, rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 14. By trusting, the road meets no barrier; one goes forth with honor, doesn't drift down side roads, and is bound to dharma.
Your line: the way opens. Today, take the one step you've been avoiding, before the day ends, and notice how the road looks from the other side. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: Pauri 15: trusting, the door of freedom
186.hook: mannai: by trust one finds the door of liberation and helps others across (Japji 15)
186.howItsDone: Pauri 15 closes the four mannai stanzas of Japji Sahib; many Sikhs connect its line about crossing and carrying others across with seva, service to others, as part of daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 14. Your line was the way opens. Did you take the step you'd been avoiding? Today, the last trusting stanza, and the end of this stretch of the path. Day one hundred eighty-six.

Picture a river crossing before bridges. Someone who knows the ford wades in, finds the stones, feels the current, and gets to the other side. That's one kind of freedom. But the people you remember are the ones who then turn around, wade back, and take a child on their shoulders, and then an old man by the arm, and then the next one. Getting across is one thing. Carrying others across is another. Pauri 15 ends the trusting stanzas with both.
screen: `A RIVER, NO BRIDGE.` → `ONE WADES ACROSS.` → `THEN TURNS BACK FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Pauri 15, in paraphrase. By trusting, one finds the door of liberation. By trusting, one lifts up one's family. By trusting, the Guru's Sikh crosses over, and carries others across. By trusting, Nanak says, one doesn't wander around begging. And the refrain one last time: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. The first line in the original is mannai paavahi mokh duaar. Mokh is the same idea as today's word, mukti: liberation, freedom. Duaar is a door. Many Indian traditions speak of liberation, and they picture it in different ways. Sikh teaching often stresses jivan mukti, being free while alive, here, in a household, with work and family, not only after death or away in a forest. And look at the very next line: by trusting, the family is lifted too. Freedom doesn't pull you out of your people. Then the line for today's carry: mannai tarai taare gur sikh. The Guru's Sikh crosses, and carries across. Tarai, crosses over. Taare, makes others cross. The same verb, turned outward. The picture is the river from the hook, and it's everywhere in Sikh scripture: the world as a sea, the Name as the boat. And the last line, not wandering around begging, is about not having to go door to door for scraps of meaning. That hunger has been met. So the whole run of eight stanzas lands here. Listen, pauris 8 to 11. Trust, 12 to 15. And trust ends not in private calm but in a door, and in turning back for someone else.
screen: `MOKH DUAAR — THE DOOR OF FREEDOM.` · `FREE WHILE ALIVE, WITH FAMILY.` · `TARAI TAARE — CROSSES, CARRIES.` · `LISTEN, THEN TRUST, THEN CARRY.` · then, large: `FREE, AND FREEING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's stuck on the near bank of something right now: a worry, a task, a hard week. Picture them clearly. Then, without solving their whole life, find one small way you could help them across today: a message, a ride, an hour, a listening ear. Hold the picture of that one act. Then rest with the breath, and let the plan settle. The bell holds the time.
Mukti. Liberation, freedom; in Sikh teaching, often freedom while alive. In Pauri 15, the one who trusts finds its door and helps others through.
Your line: free, and freeing. Today, do the one small thing you pictured, and help one person across something. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: Pauri 16, sound: panch parvaan
187.tomorrow: Pauri 16, meaning: the bull is dharma
187.howItsDone: Pauri 16 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning by many Sikhs; its opening line, panch parvaan panch pardhaan, marks the turn from the listening and trusting stanzas to the longer stanzas on creation's countlessness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mukti, and the end of the trusting stanzas. Your line was free, and freeing. Did you help one person across something? Today, a new stretch of Japji begins. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

For eight stanzas, Japji has been a drumbeat of one word: suniai, suniai, suniai, then mannai, mannai, mannai. Short lines, the same opening every time. Now the music changes. Pauri 16 is longer, wider, and it opens with a line you can almost clap to. Say it and it snaps: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan. Two halves, like two footsteps. After this, the stanzas start counting the uncountable: worlds, devotions, fools, names. This week and next are called the countless. But first, today, just the sound of the door into it.
screen: `SUNIAI, MANNAI — A DRUMBEAT.` → `THE MUSIC CHANGES.` → `PANCH PARVAAN, PANCH PARDHAAN.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening line in the original: panch parvaan panch pardhaan. Four words, and two of them the same. Panch, said PUNCH, is the key word. It can mean five, and it also means the chosen ones, the respected ones, the way a village council in Punjab was called a panchayat. Most Sikh commentators hear it here as the chosen ones: people who have listened and trusted, the ones the last eight stanzas were describing. We'll open that more tomorrow. Parvaan, par-VAAN: accepted, approved, the way a coin is accepted as genuine. Pardhaan, par-DHAAN: foremost, the chief. It's the same word Punjabis still use for the president of a committee. So: the chosen are accepted; the chosen are foremost. Now the next three lines, in paraphrase: the chosen receive honor in the Court of God; the chosen shine even at the doors of kings; the chosen keep their attention on the one Guru. Listen to how the line is built. Panch opens both halves, like a bell struck twice. Parvaan and pardhaan rhyme, both ending on the long aan. That's why it's easy to say and hard to forget. People who recite Japji every morning feel the stanza shift here, from the steady beat of the last eight into something that stretches out. Pauri 16 goes on to talk about a bull holding up the earth, and about countless worlds. That's tomorrow. For today, just get the first line into your mouth.
screen: `PANCH — THE CHOSEN ONES.` · `PARVAAN — ACCEPTED.` · `PARDHAAN — FOREMOST.` · `A BELL STRUCK TWICE.` · then, large: `PANCH PARVAAN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan. Slowly the first time, feeling each syllable. Then again, letting the two halves fall like footsteps. Say it three or four times, then let the words go quiet and sit with the rhythm still moving in you. If a thought comes, let panch parvaan bring you back. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 16. It opens with panch parvaan, panch pardhaan: the chosen are accepted, the chosen are foremost.
Your line: panch parvaan. Today, say the line once more while you're walking somewhere, matching the two halves to your steps. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

188.title: Pauri 16, meaning: the bull is dharma
188.hook: the earth is held not by a bull but by dharma, born of compassion; with one word the whole creation spread (Japji 16)
188.howItsDone: Pauri 16 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; its line dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot is often quoted by Sikhs to say that the world is upheld by righteousness born of compassion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 16. Your line was panch parvaan: the chosen are accepted. Did the line walk with you? Today, what the chosen understand. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Every child eventually asks it: what holds up the world? In Guru Nanak's India, one answer people told was a bull. The earth rests on the back of a great bull, and when it shifts its weight, the ground shakes. It's a picture many cultures have had in some form: a turtle, a giant, an elephant, something strong underneath everything. Pauri 16 picks up that bull, turns it over in its hands, and gives it a new meaning. It's one of the most quoted lines in Japji.
screen: `WHAT HOLDS UP THE WORLD?` → `A GREAT BULL, PEOPLE SAID.` → `NANAK TURNS IT OVER.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we met the panch, the chosen ones, the people who have listened and trusted. Today the stanza tells us what they understand. Here's the line in the original: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. Dhaul is the bull. Dharam is dharma, right living, the moral order. Daiaa is compassion, and poot is son. The bull is dharma, the son of compassion. And the next line, in paraphrase: contentment, santokh, the word from a week ago, holds it patiently in place. So what holds up the world? Not an animal. Right living. And right living is born from compassion, and steadied by contentment. Then the stanza asks the obvious question, almost with a smile. If a bull held up the earth, what would hold up the bull? Beyond this earth there are more earths, and more beyond those. What strength could carry all that weight? The bull can't be the answer, because it just moves the question down one level. Then Pauri 16 widens out. All the beings, of every kind and color and name, were written by the ever-flowing pen. Who could ever write that account? With a single word, the whole creation spread out, and from it flowed countless rivers. And it closes with a refrain we'll hear for four stanzas: what power do I have to describe it? Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One. That's the understanding of the panch. The world stands on compassion, and it came from one word.
screen: `DHAUL DHARAM DAIAA KAA POOT.` · `WHAT HOLDS UP THE BULL?` · `ONE WORD, COUNTLESS RIVERS.` · `WHATEVER PLEASES YOU IS GOOD.` · then, large: `COMPASSION HOLDS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Think of one act of compassion you could do today, small and real. Someone who's tired, someone who's alone, someone who's struggling with something you could lighten. Picture doing it: what you'd say, what your hands would do. Let the feeling of it rest in your chest. Then sit and breathe, feeling the ground under you, and let it remind you what the stanza says holds it up. The bell holds the time.
Panch. The chosen ones of Pauri 16, who understand that the bull holding up the world is dharma, the son of compassion.
Your line: compassion holds the world. Today, do the one act of compassion you pictured, and let it be part of what holds things up. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

what it means: what holds the world up is right living, born of compassion and steadied by contentment.

189.title: Pauri 17: countless devotions
189.hook: asankh jap: countless prayers, loves, worships and austerities; whatever pleases You is good (Japji 17)
189.howItsDone: Pauri 17 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 17 to 19 each repeat asankh, countless, and many Sikhs recite them with a steady, rolling rhythm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the panch and the bull. Your line was compassion holds the world. Did your one act of compassion happen? Today, the end of a week, and a word that can't be counted. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

First, the week behind us. No pen for this: trust can't be written down. Surat: trust wakes you. The way opens. Mukti: free, and freeing. Then panch parvaan, and compassion holding the world. Now, try this tonight: go outside and count the stars. You'll get to forty, lose your place, start again, and give up. Not because you're bad at counting, but because the thing is bigger than numbers. There's a word for that feeling. Pauri 17 uses it eight times in eight lines.

segments.voice: The word is asankh. A means not. Sankh means number, count. Asankh: without number, countless. And Pauri 17 is a list that keeps saying it. Its first line in the original: asankh jap asankh bhaau. Countless are the meditations, countless the loves. Then, in paraphrase: countless worships, countless austerities. Countless scriptures, and people reciting the Vedas. Countless yogis whose minds stay detached from the world. Countless devotees reflecting on virtue and wisdom. Countless people who are truthful, countless who are generous. Countless warriors who face the steel. Countless silent sages, their attention held in love. Notice what's in that list. Vedic recitation. Yogis. Silent sages. Warriors. Givers. It gathers the devotion of many different kinds of people, from many ways of life, and it doesn't rank them. It just keeps saying: countless, countless. And then the refrain we heard begin yesterday: what power do I have to describe it? Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One. That's today's line: countless, and good. The stanza isn't impressed by numbers for their own sake. It's pointing past them. However many ways people devote themselves, and they are beyond counting, the measure of good isn't the count. It's what pleases the One. Some Sikh teachers hear a quiet freedom in that. You don't have to out-pray or out-give anyone. You're one of the countless. And that is good.
screen: `A-SANKH — WITHOUT NUMBER.` · `ASANKH JAP ASANKH BHAAU.` · `MANY WAYS, NONE RANKED.` · `WHATEVER PLEASES YOU IS GOOD.` · then, large: `COUNTLESS, AND GOOD.`

segments.voice: Count ten breaths, then stop. One on the out-breath, two on the next, all the way to ten. If you lose count, start again at one, gently. When you reach ten, stop counting. Just keep breathing, without numbers, and notice that the breaths go on whether you count them or not. Rest there, in the uncounted ones. The bell holds the time.
Asankh. A, not; sankh, number. Countless. Pauri 17 uses it for the devotions of every kind of person, and ranks none of them.
Your line: countless, and good. Today, when you see someone's way of devotion that isn't yours, a prayer, a fast, a quiet habit, let it be one of the countless. Day one hundred eighty-nine.
